rv.q: The implicit optimism of this gesture extends the sad peace of the play’s finale into a world where, for all our divisions, love is possible again.
It's a shame to feel so little in a show that's bent on giving us so much to look at.
This “Romeo and Juliet” undoes itself through conflicting, increasingly haphazard choices.
What these leading players lack in experience they make up for with energy and enthusiasm.

June 11, 2026: Many years ago when I was acting in a community theater production of The Skin of Our Teeth, one of my castmates railed against an all-African-American, Off-Broadway production of The Cherry Orchard, claiming black actors did have the “cultural background” to perform Anton Chekhov’s classic of displacement in a Russian family.

And while I have no issue with relocating or updating the Bard's works, this particular choice ultimately detracts more than adds to the proceedings. First, Maruti Evans' set, decidedly stark and littered with crosses, is rather bland viewing for nearly three hours.
No answers abound in this Romeo & Juliet, an aesthetically-pleasing, well-acted production that cannot find a thesis statement in English or in Spanish.
Romeo and Juliet, is a letdown.

But the production, which uncomfortably grafts this highly specific contemporary gloss onto the now-bilingual text, is both heavy-handed and incoherent, and more likely to provoke eye-rolls than demonstrations.

A vibrant, entertaining evening of Shakespeare- that could be so much more so.

cn.t: This politically charged production, set against the border wall, draws mixed-to-negative reviews for its heavy-handed concept, though critics praise the chemistry between the leads in their intimate scenes.
